title: Mode demarcation and traffic handling primer
content:
Purpose:
This primer captures a compact, operationally-focused view of how traffic should be handled across Redwood’s three serving modes (hosted, dedicated, private). It is intended for platform engineers and SREs who need an actionable demarcation of ownership, routing behavior, and failure handling rather than a long-form design doc.

Goals:
- Make ownership of request paths explicit for developers and SREs.
- Provide a consistent fallback story across modes for graceful degradation.
- Define practical isolation controls (network, compute, logical) that can be implemented with our current infra.
- Surface a minimal set of monitoring signals and runbook steps for triage.

Assumptions and constraints:
- We support three primary modes: Hosted (shared, multi-tenant service endpoints), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools and ingress isolation per customer), Private (customer-controlled network; control plane may be isolated).
- We must preserve low-latency for latency-sensitive routes while enabling cost-optimized fallbacks.
- Customers may pin models or accept a compatible fallback variant.

Short glossary:
- Edge router: public-facing gateway that accepts client requests (hosted only; dedicated/private can have an edge in a customer VPC).
- Control plane: central orchestration and routing decision service (may be multi-tenant or tenant-scoped depending on mode).
- Data plane: GPU clusters and inference runtime that execute requests.
- Fallback variant: a compatible model/version used when primary capacity is unavailable.

High-level demarcation by mode (operational view):
1) Hosted (default, shared):
   - Control plane: multi-tenant global control plane. Responsible for routing, model catalog, quota enforcement, and global failover decisions.
   - Routing behavior: requests hit public edge -> global control plane decides region/pool based on latency, cost policy, and tenant tier -> route to shared pool (possibly region-local).
   - Isolation: logical isolation via per-tenant tokens, rate limits, resource quotas, and runtime request fencing (RBAC + request metadata). No network-level tenant segregation by default.
   - Fallbacks: automatic fallback to cheaper model variants or other regions according to policy.
   - Failure modes: systemic capacity shortage triggers prioritized shedding + fallbacks.

2) Dedicated (reserved capacity for a tenant):
   - Control plane: shared control plane with tenant-aware routing decisions; routing can be delegated to a tenant-specific routing layer for ingress affinity.
   - Routing behavior: edge -> control plane retains routing, but routes preferentially to the tenant’s reserved pools. If reserved pool is saturated, policy options: queue, spillover to shared pools (if customer allows), or fail fast.
   - Isolation: compute isolation (dedicated GPU instances/pools) + stronger tenancy quotas. Network egress/ingress is still managed by our VPCs unless customer has private options.
   - Fallbacks: by contract — spillover only when explicitly allowed; otherwise automatic degradation (reject/queue) with SLA signals.

3) Private (customer-managed network or on-prem):
   - Control plane: two patterns: (A) central control plane with tenant-scoped decision endpoints inside customer VPC (control plane proxy), or (B) fully air-gapped control plane running customer-managed components.
   - Routing behavior: requests ingress at customer boundary -> local control plane/proxy makes local routing decisions -> data plane local to customer. Cross-region options must be explicit (cross-site federation).
   - Isolation: full network-level separation; optionally separate control plane. Storage and telemetry may be sharded or proxied to central observability depending on compliance.
   - Fallbacks: minimal automatic fallback; failover across regions is allowed only if explicitly configured and authorized.

Concrete routing policy primitives (proposal):
- Affinity(policy): {prefer_reserved, prefer_same_region, lowest_latency, cost_preference}.
- Spill(action): {deny, queue, spill_to_shared, spill_to_variant}.
- ControlPlaneScope: {global, tenant_scoped, local_proxy}.
- TelemetryForwarding: {always, telemetry_via_proxy, disabled}.

Example policies by mode:
- Hosted default: Affinity = lowest_latency; Spill = spill_to_variant; ControlPlaneScope = global; TelemetryForwarding = always.
- Dedicated (strict): Affinity = prefer_reserved; Spill = deny (or queue if configured); ControlPlaneScope = global (tenant-aware); TelemetryForwarding = always.
- Private (sovereign): Affinity = prefer_local; Spill = deny; ControlPlaneScope = local_proxy; TelemetryForwarding = telemetry_via_proxy or disabled.

Multi-region considerations (behavior matrix):
- Latency-first routes: prefer region-local pools. If latency SLO violated and policy allows, escalate to inter-region route with explicit tagging (so we can bill/track).
- Capacity-driven spill: if region lacks capacity, use control plane to either: queue, use a fallback variant, or route to a different region. Routing across regions must carry headers: X-Orig-Region, X-Fallback-Reason, X-Tenant-Consent.
- Data residency: for private mode, do not cross region boundaries unless tenant policy allows and encryption/audit guarantees are present.

Operational runbook (triage checklist):
- Symptom: 5xx increase for a tenant in Hosted mode.
  1) Check tenant quota/usage in control plane (quota_exhausted?).
  2) Verify edges: TLS/ALB errors, certificate issues.
  3) Inspect pool-level metrics: GPU saturation, OOMs, runtime latencies.
  4) Check fallback events: did control plane choose a variant? Why? (policy audit log).
  5) If systemic capacity exhaustion, enable temporary shed policies (reduce batch sizes, reduce model concurrency) and notify customer about degraded variant.

- Symptom: requests for a Dedicated tenant are routed to shared pools.
  1) Confirm tenant reserved pool status and autoscaler health.
  2) Verify routing annotations on control plane for that tenant (spill allowed?).
  3) Check network path: Is the edge forwarding to the correct pool or was a health check diversion triggered?

- Symptom: Private deployment cross-region leak observed.
  1) Confirm telemetry and egress ACLs in tenant VPC.
  2) Review control plane proxy config and federated routing rules.
  3) Engage compliance to run forensic on data plane copies.

Monitoring signals (minimum):
- Per-tenant: request rate, p50/p95 latency, token cost per request, 5xx rate, quota remaining, fallback count (per type).
- Pool-level: GPU utilization, queue length, batch size distribution, average KV cache hit ratio.
- Control plane: routing decision latency, policy-evaluation failures, health of region maps and peering.

Quick wins and low-effort enforcements (implementation suggestions):
- Emit explicit headers on every routed request to carry routing provenance (region, pool-id, decision-reason).
- Add a single boolean on tenant profile: allow_spill_to_shared. Use it immediately to avoid accidental spill.
- Centralize policy evaluation logs for a 7-day window for debug (keep only metadata for private deployments).
- Default hosted behavior: prefer variant fallbacks over cross-region routing to limit egress and keep latency predictable.

Open questions and discussion items for next sync:
- How aggressive should automatic cross-region routing be when a single region is degraded? (cost/latency tradeoffs)
- For Dedicated customers, should we support a soft-spill mode that bills at a premium when using shared pools?
- In Private on-prem installs, what is the minimum telemetry we must collect for product iteration while still satisfying compliance?

Appendix: short sample header contract sent by control plane when routing cross-region:
- X-RD-Origin-Region: <region-id>
- X-RD-Orig-Pool: <pool-id>
- X-RD-Decision: <primary|fallback|spill>
- X-RD-Fallback-Reason: <quota|capacity|latency|health>

Notes and references:
- Related tickets: JIRA-PLAT-789 (spilling policy), JIRA-PLAT-812 (private telemetry contract).
- Existing confluence: PLAT-traffic-patterns (see linked artifact).

Author: Avery Chen (eng-platform) — draft for review.
